questions.question: Which ancient Celtic festival is widely seen as a root of Halloween?
questions.fun_fact: Samhain marked the end of the harvest and the start of the dark half of the year. It is pronounced roughly 'SOW-in'.

questions.question: What does the word 'Halloween' originally mean?

answers.text: The evening before All Hallows' Day
The night of the harvest moon

questions.fun_fact: 'Hallow' is an old word for a saint, and 'e'en' is a contraction of 'evening' — All Hallows' Day is All Saints' Day on 1 November.

questions.question: Before pumpkins took over, what did people in Ireland and Scotland carve into lanterns?
questions.fun_fact: Irish immigrants in North America switched to the native pumpkin, which was bigger and far easier to hollow out.

questions.question: In the Irish folk tale behind the name 'jack-o'-lantern', whom does Stingy Jack trick?
questions.fun_fact: Turned away from both heaven and hell, Jack is said to wander the night with a glowing coal inside a carved turnip.

questions.question: In Scotland, what did 'guising' children traditionally have to do before receiving a treat?

answers.text: Perform a song, poem or joke

questions.fun_fact: The name comes from 'disguise'. In parts of Scotland children are still expected to do a turn before the sweets come out.

questions.question: What was the medieval custom of poor people going door to door, offering prayers for the dead in exchange for small cakes?
questions.fun_fact: The little pastries were called soul cakes, and each one eaten was said to help a soul out of purgatory.

questions.question: In a Victorian Halloween fortune-telling game, what did a young woman hope to see after eating an apple in front of a mirror?
questions.fun_fact: Done by candlelight, often at midnight, the future sweetheart's face was supposed to appear over her shoulder in the glass.

questions.question: The earliest known printed use of the phrase 'trick or treat', from 1927, appeared in a newspaper from which country?
questions.fun_fact: The report came from the small town of Blackie in Alberta, where children demanded 'edible plunder' at front and back doors.

questions.question: What held back Halloween treats in the United States during World War II?
questions.fun_fact: Children got peanuts, coins or popcorn balls instead of sweets; US sugar rationing only ended in 1947.

questions.question: Mexico's Día de Muertos, celebrated right after Halloween, is mainly about what?

answers.text: Welcoming back the souls of loved ones who have died

questions.fun_fact: It is its own tradition, not a Mexican Halloween: families build home altars called ofrendas with photos and favourite foods, and UNESCO lists it as intangible cultural heritage.

questions.question: Which bright orange flower is used on Día de Muertos to guide the souls to the family altars?
questions.fun_fact: In Mexico the marigold is called cempasúchil; its strong scent and colour are believed to lead the spirits home.

questions.question: According to Samhain tradition, what happened on that night?

answers.text: The boundary between this world and the Otherworld grew thin
The sun stood still in the sky
Crops planted that night grew twice as fast

questions.fun_fact: Bonfires were lit, and later folklore says people wore disguises so wandering spirits would not recognise them.

questions.question: Which city hosts the Village Halloween Parade, where anyone in costume can march?
questions.fun_fact: It started in Greenwich Village in 1974 as a walk for a puppeteer's children and their neighbours.

questions.question: Which Massachusetts town, famous for its witch trials of 1692, draws huge crowds every October?
questions.fun_fact: Despite the legends, none of those executed in Salem was burned at the stake — nineteen people were hanged.

questions.question: Which traditional Irish Halloween fruit bread has a ring baked inside?
questions.fun_fact: Finding the ring was said to mean a wedding within a year; other tokens such as a coin or a pea foretold wealth or poverty.

questions.question: Under which name was candy corn marketed around 1900?
questions.fun_fact: Back then corn was seen as animal fodder, so the joke name fit; old boxes even showed a rooster.

questions.question: Which US state grows by far the most pumpkins?
questions.fun_fact: Most of them end up in cans: a single factory in Morton, Illinois, processes the bulk of America's canned pumpkin.

questions.question: Botanically speaking, what is a pumpkin?
questions.fun_fact: It grows from a flower and holds its seeds inside, making it a kind of berry botanists call a pepo.

questions.question: Which plant family do pumpkins belong to?

answers.text: The gourd family, with cucumbers and melons

questions.fun_fact: Courgettes, butternut squash and watermelons are close relatives too.

questions.question: What is classic 'pumpkin spice' seasoning made of?
questions.fun_fact: It is named after the pie it flavours, which is why many pumpkin spice products contain no pumpkin at all.

questions.question: Who wrote 'Frankenstein'?
questions.fun_fact: She started the story at 18 during a ghost-story contest with Lord Byron and friends at Lake Geneva in 1816.

questions.question: What is the monster's name in Mary Shelley's novel 'Frankenstein'?
questions.fun_fact: Victor Frankenstein is the scientist who builds him — and a hunchbacked assistant called Igor appears in neither the novel nor the 1931 film.

questions.question: The eruption of which volcano caused the gloomy 1816 summer that kept Mary Shelley's group indoors telling ghost stories?
questions.fun_fact: The 1815 eruption in Indonesia cooled the whole planet, and 1816 became known as the 'Year Without a Summer'.

questions.question: Which early vampire story grew out of the same 1816 ghost-story contest that produced 'Frankenstein'?
questions.fun_fact: Polidori was Lord Byron's personal doctor, and his elegant vampire Lord Ruthven was modelled on Byron himself.

questions.question: Who wrote 'Dracula'?
questions.fun_fact: Stoker was Irish and worked for years as business manager of London's Lyceum Theatre.

questions.question: In which region does Count Dracula have his castle?
questions.fun_fact: Bran Castle in Romania is marketed as Dracula's castle, although Stoker never visited Romania.

questions.question: Which real ruler's family name is linked to the name 'Dracula'?
questions.fun_fact: 'Dracula' means 'son of the dragon' — his father belonged to a knightly society called the Order of the Dragon.

questions.question: In Stoker's novel, where does Dracula come ashore in England?
questions.fun_fact: He arrives on a wrecked ship and leaps ashore in the shape of a large dog; Whitby now hosts popular goth weekends.

questions.question: In Edgar Allan Poe's poem 'The Raven', which word does the bird keep repeating?
questions.fun_fact: Poe lived and died in Baltimore, whose NFL team, the Ravens, was named after the poem.

questions.question: In which Edgar Allan Poe story is the narrator driven mad by a beating heart under the floorboards?
questions.fun_fact: Poe is also credited with inventing the modern detective story with 'The Murders in the Rue Morgue' in 1841.

questions.question: In 'The Legend of Sleepy Hollow', who is the Headless Horseman said to be?

answers.text: The ghost of a Hessian soldier
A Dutch farmer who lost a bet

questions.fun_fact: In 1996 the village of North Tarrytown, New York, voted to rename itself Sleepy Hollow.

questions.question: In Robert Louis Stevenson's 1886 novella, what is the name of Dr Jekyll's evil alter ego?
questions.fun_fact: Stevenson said the core of the story came to him in a dream.

questions.question: In Oscar Wilde's 'The Picture of Dorian Gray', what grows old instead of Dorian?
questions.fun_fact: It is the only novel Oscar Wilde ever wrote.

questions.question: Who wrote 'The Haunting of Hill House' (1959)?
questions.fun_fact: Jackson is also famous for the short story 'The Lottery', which prompted a flood of angry letters to The New Yorker in 1948.

questions.question: In which US state are most of Stephen King's stories set?
questions.fun_fact: King lives in Bangor, Maine, where the iron fence of his house is decorated with bats and spiders.

questions.question: In Roald Dahl's 'The Witches', what does the Grand High Witch plan to turn children into?
questions.fun_fact: Dahl's real witches are bald under their wigs and have square feet with no toes.

questions.question: In the first Harry Potter book, what gets loose inside Hogwarts on Halloween?
questions.fun_fact: Halloween is a dark date in the series: Harry's parents died on 31 October 1981.

questions.question: In which city is 'The Phantom of the Opera' set?
questions.fun_fact: The Palais Garnier opera house really does have a water tank beneath it, which inspired the Phantom's underground lake.

questions.question: Which vampire novella with a female vampire appeared 25 years before 'Dracula'?
questions.fun_fact: Its author, Sheridan Le Fanu, was Irish like Bram Stoker, and 'Carmilla' is often named as an influence on 'Dracula'.

questions.question: The mask in John Carpenter's 'Halloween' was originally a cheap mask of which character?
questions.fun_fact: The crew bought it for about two dollars, spray-painted it white and stretched out the eye holes.

questions.question: Who composed the eerie piano theme of John Carpenter's 'Halloween'?
questions.fun_fact: The theme is in the unusual 5/4 time signature, which helps give it its restless feel.

questions.question: Who sang the 1984 hit 'Ghostbusters'?
questions.fun_fact: Huey Lewis claimed it sounded too much like his 'I Want a New Drug', and the dispute was settled out of court.

questions.question: What is the giant marshmallow monster in 'Ghostbusters' called?
questions.fun_fact: Ray tried to empty his mind and thought of the most harmless thing he could remember from childhood — which then attacked New York.

questions.question: Which horror film legend performs the spoken part at the end of Michael Jackson's 'Thriller'?
questions.fun_fact: The music video, directed by John Landis, runs nearly 14 minutes — more like a short film.

questions.question: Who recorded the 1962 novelty hit 'Monster Mash'?
questions.fun_fact: The BBC banned it as 'too morbid'; it only reached the UK top ten when re-released in 1973.

questions.question: Who is the Pumpkin King in 'The Nightmare Before Christmas'?
questions.fun_fact: The film was directed by Henry Selick; Tim Burton came up with the story and produced it.

questions.question: What are the three witches in Disney's 'Hocus Pocus' called?
questions.fun_fact: The Halloween film was released in July 1993, flopped, and only became a classic through years of TV repeats.

questions.question: In 'It's the Great Pumpkin, Charlie Brown', what does Charlie Brown get at every house when trick-or-treating?
questions.fun_fact: After the first broadcast in 1966, sympathetic viewers mailed sweets to the Peanuts studio for Charlie Brown.

questions.question: What is the name of the disembodied hand in 'The Addams Family'?
questions.fun_fact: The family began as single-panel cartoons by Charles Addams in The New Yorker in 1938.

questions.question: Who played the monster in Universal's 1931 film 'Frankenstein'?
questions.fun_fact: Karloff was born William Henry Pratt in London, and the flat-headed make-up took hours to apply each day.

questions.question: Who played the title role in Universal's 1931 film 'Dracula'?
questions.fun_fact: Lugosi was Hungarian and had already played Dracula on Broadway; he was buried in one of his Dracula capes.

questions.question: What is the vampire called in the 1922 German silent film 'Nosferatu'?
questions.fun_fact: The studio never got the rights to 'Dracula', and Bram Stoker's widow won a court order that copies be destroyed — luckily some survived.

questions.question: What did Alfred Hitchcock use as fake blood in the black-and-white film 'Psycho'?
questions.fun_fact: In black and white, chocolate syrup looked more convincing than anything red, and it flowed just right.

questions.question: How many times must you say 'Beetlejuice' to summon him?
questions.fun_fact: Michael Keaton is on screen for only about 17 minutes of the 92-minute 1988 film.

questions.question: In 'Gremlins', after what time must you never feed a mogwai?
questions.fun_fact: Gizmo's squeaky voice was provided by comedian Howie Mandel.

questions.question: In Pixar's 'Coco', set on Día de Muertos, what does Miguel dream of becoming?
questions.fun_fact: His dog Dante is a Xoloitzcuintli, the ancient Mexican hairless dog breed.

questions.question: How is E.T. disguised when the children smuggle him out on Halloween?

answers.text: As a ghost under a sheet

questions.fun_fact: On the way he spots a child dressed as Yoda and seems to recognise him — a nod from Spielberg to his friend George Lucas.

questions.question: In which US state is the town of Hawkins from 'Stranger Things' set?
questions.fun_fact: Season 2 opens on Halloween 1984, and the boys go trick-or-treating dressed as the Ghostbusters.

questions.question: Who almost always turns out to be behind the 'monster' in 'Scooby-Doo'?
questions.fun_fact: Unmasked villains famously complain they would have got away with it, if it weren't for those meddling kids.

questions.question: Who composed 'Night on Bald Mountain', used for the demon scene in Disney's 'Fantasia'?
questions.fun_fact: The version most people know was reworked by Nikolai Rimsky-Korsakov after Mussorgsky's death.

questions.question: In Saint-Saëns' 'Danse macabre', which instrument imitates rattling skeleton bones?
questions.fun_fact: Death's solo violin has its top string tuned down to E-flat, giving it a deliberately sour sound.

questions.question: Which composer is credited with the organ 'Toccata and Fugue in D minor' heard in so many haunted-house scenes?
questions.fun_fact: Some musicologists doubt Bach really wrote it, but it is still published under his name.

questions.question: What are The Simpsons' yearly Halloween episodes called?
questions.fun_fact: The first one aired in October 1990, during the show's second season.

questions.question: In folklore and film, what is supposed to kill a werewolf?
questions.fun_fact: The full moon as the trigger for transformation was mostly fixed by 20th-century films; older legends used curses or magic belts.

questions.question: According to folklore, what can't a vampire see in a mirror?
questions.fun_fact: One explanation offered for the legend is the old belief that mirrors show the soul — and vampires are said to have none.

questions.question: According to Prague legend, which rabbi made a Golem out of clay?
questions.fun_fact: The creature was brought to life with the Hebrew word 'emet' (truth); rubbing out the first letter left 'met' (dead) and stopped it.

questions.question: In Irish folklore, what does the wail of a banshee announce?
questions.fun_fact: The name comes from the Irish 'bean sí', meaning 'woman of the fairy mound'.

questions.question: What does the name of the legendary creature 'chupacabra' mean?
questions.fun_fact: The first widely reported sightings came from Puerto Rico in 1995.

questions.question: In Slavic folklore, what does the witch Baba Yaga's hut stand on?
questions.fun_fact: She doesn't ride a broom either: she flies in a giant mortar and steers with a pestle.

questions.question: How do you defeat a kappa, the water creature of Japanese folklore?

answers.text: Bow to it, so it bows back and spills the water from its head

questions.fun_fact: Kappa are said to love cucumbers, which is why a cucumber sushi roll is called kappamaki.

questions.question: Which country's folklore gave the world the zombie?
questions.fun_fact: The first feature-length zombie film was 'White Zombie' from 1932, starring Bela Lugosi and set in Haiti.

questions.question: Which organ did ancient Egyptian embalmers usually leave inside a mummy?
questions.fun_fact: The heart was believed to be weighed against a feather in the afterlife to judge the dead person's life.

questions.question: In English folklore, what is a will-o'-the-wisp?

answers.text: A ghostly light that lures travellers off the path

questions.fun_fact: One suggested scientific explanation for the flickering lights over marshes is gas from rotting plants catching fire.

questions.question: Which figure of Irish folklore rides a black horse and carries its own head?
questions.fun_fact: According to legend the Dullahan is terrified of gold — even a small gold pin can drive it away.

questions.question: What does the German word 'poltergeist' mean?
questions.fun_fact: Poltergeists are blamed for banging, flying objects and moving furniture rather than for appearing as figures.

questions.question: The ghost ship 'Flying Dutchman' is said to be doomed to sail forever off which cape?
questions.fun_fact: Richard Wagner turned the legend into his opera 'The Flying Dutchman', first performed in 1843.

questions.question: How does the jiangshi, a 'hopping vampire' of Chinese folklore, get around?

answers.text: By hopping with its arms stretched out
By flying on a bat's wings

questions.fun_fact: Its stiff body is linked to rigor mortis, which is why it can't walk and has to hop.

questions.question: According to German legend, on which mountain do witches gather on Walpurgis Night?
questions.fun_fact: Goethe set a wild Walpurgis Night scene on the Brocken in 'Faust'; the night is celebrated on 30 April.

questions.question: Which is the only mammal capable of true powered flight?
questions.fun_fact: There are more than 1,400 bat species — roughly one in five of all mammal species.

questions.question: How do many bats find their way and their food in total darkness?
questions.fun_fact: Not all bats echolocate: most fruit bats rely on their good eyesight and sense of smell.

questions.question: Where in the world do vampire bats live?
questions.fun_fact: There are only three species, and they share meals with roost-mates that went hungry that night.

questions.question: How good is a bat's eyesight?

answers.text: No bat is blind — all species can see

questions.fun_fact: 'Blind as a bat' is a myth; some large fruit bats see very well in dim light.

questions.question: Spiders are not insects. Which animal group do they belong to?
questions.fun_fact: Scorpions, ticks and mites are arachnids too — all with eight legs.

questions.question: What is the fear of spiders called?
questions.fun_fact: Acrophobia is the fear of heights and agoraphobia the fear of places where escape feels hard.

questions.question: What is the fear of Halloween sometimes called?
questions.fun_fact: The fear of ghosts has its own name too: phasmophobia.

questions.question: What causes goosebumps when you get a fright?

answers.text: Tiny muscles at the base of hairs pulling them upright

questions.fun_fact: In furry animals the same reflex fluffs up the coat and makes them look bigger to an enemy.

questions.question: Which hormone floods your body during a sudden scare?
questions.fun_fact: It speeds up your heart and widens your pupils to let in more light — the classic 'fight or flight' response.

questions.question: What allows owls to fly almost silently?

answers.text: Comb-like edges on their wing feathers

questions.fun_fact: Engineers copied the design to make quieter fans and to cut the noise of Japanese bullet trains.

questions.question: How do many American tarantulas defend themselves?

answers.text: By flicking irritating hairs off their bodies

questions.fun_fact: The barbed hairs cause itching and can be very unpleasant in the eyes or nose of a predator.

questions.question: What happens to scorpions under ultraviolet light?
questions.fun_fact: A substance in their outer shell causes the glow, and scientists still debate what it is good for.

questions.question: What did researchers at the University of Washington show about crows?

answers.text: They remember faces of people who threatened them
They can see in total darkness

questions.fun_fact: Years later the crows still scolded the 'dangerous' mask — even birds that had never seen it before joined in.

questions.question: What is a group of crows called?
questions.fun_fact: A parliament is a group of owls, and a pride is a group of lions.

questions.question: What is the full moon after the Harvest Moon traditionally called?
questions.fun_fact: It usually falls in October; the Wolf Moon is January's full moon and the Snow Moon February's.

questions.question: Which plant was said to scream when pulled out of the ground?
questions.fun_fact: Its forked root can look like a little human figure, which fed the legend — and Harry Potter's Herbology lessons.

questions.question: Which moth has a pattern like a skull on its back?
questions.fun_fact: It can squeak loudly when disturbed and sneaks into beehives to steal honey.

questions.question: Which nocturnal lemur with a long, thin middle finger is traditionally seen as a bad omen in parts of Madagascar?
questions.fun_fact: It taps on tree bark with that finger and listens for hollow spots where grubs are hiding.

questions.question: How many bones are there in an adult human skeleton?
questions.fun_fact: 206 — a newborn has around 300, but many of them fuse together as the child grows.

questions.question: In which year was Bram Stoker's 'Dracula' first published?
questions.fun_fact: 1897. The whole novel is told through letters, diary entries and newspaper clippings.

questions.question: In which year did the silent vampire film 'Nosferatu' premiere?
questions.fun_fact: 1922, in Berlin. The shadow of Count Orlok creeping up the stairs is still one of cinema's most copied images.

questions.question: In which year did Martin Luther post his 95 theses — on 31 October, the eve of All Saints' Day?
questions.fun_fact: 1517. That is why Germany's Protestant regions celebrate Reformation Day on the very same date as Halloween.

questions.question: In which year was John Carpenter's film 'Halloween' released?
questions.fun_fact: 1978. It was shot in about three weeks in spring in California, so the crew painted paper leaves to fake autumn.
